Belgium: Prime Minister Bart De Wever offers to resign after budget talks collapse

On Monday 2 November 2026, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever tendered his resignation to King Philippe after budget talks within his coalition failed. The king has not decided: he is consulting party leaders and will see De Wever again on Friday [1][2][3].

The government's budget negotiations failed overnight between Sunday and Monday. Bart De Wever then offered his resignation to King Philippe, according to the palace, which says it follows the failure of talks within the government [1][2][3].

The king is withholding his decision. He is consulting the heads of the parliamentary groups from Tuesday, then will receive the Prime Minister at the palace again on Friday. He urged the parties to put the general interest and a spirit of compromise first [3][4].
The government is seeking €10 billion in savings by 2029 to cut a public deficit that exceeds 5% of gross domestic product [3][4].

The plan relies mainly on spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and includes a VAT increase. The MR, the French-speaking liberal party in the coalition, opposes it: it says a new tax would fuel inflation [5].
Markets reacted: the gap between Belgian and German ten-year bond yields rose above 1 percentage point. Belgium's central bank projects the deficit rising to 5.7% of GDP in 2028 [4].
If the king accepts the resignation, new elections could be called; forming another government on the balance of power from the last election also remains possible [3].

Key point: a government is falling over one number, €10 billion in savings, and Belgium risks paying more to finance its debt. When the gap with Germany exceeds 1 point, the Belgian state borrows at a higher rate than its neighbour, and every extra point of interest weighs on a deficit already above 5% of GDP [4].

The disagreement is about how to repair the accounts. A VAT rise brings in money quickly but raises prices for everyone; the MR liberals reject it for exactly that reason [5]. The palace warned that the country cannot afford a long political crisis [5].

For now nothing is settled: the outcome depends on the king's consultations this week and his new meeting with De Wever on Friday. If the parties cannot agree on the €10 billion in savings, the country risks having no clear budget, and markets will watch every step [3][4].

If you live in Europe, what happens in Brussels matters: the city hosts the European Union's institutions, and a member country whose debt worries markets can pull its neighbours' rates up. Watch the yield gap with Germany: it is the thermometer of this crisis.

news.2026-11-03-chine-bourse-rachats-act: China: after its worst month in ten years, the stock market gets permanent support from Beijing, but investors remain cold

Beijing is making its lending to companies for buying back their own shares permanent, and cutting its rate to 1%. The CSI 300 lost 8.5% in October, its worst month in more than a decade. Monday's gains faded on Tuesday [1][2][3].

The People's Bank of China (PBOC), the banking regulator (NFRA) and the securities regulator (CSRC) announced that the lending facility for share buybacks and stake increases becomes a long-term tool rather than a temporary one. Its rate falls from 1.25% to 1% [2].

The signed amount of these loans is about 440 billion yuan, of which more than 280 billion has already been paid out. The swap facility for securities firms, funds and insurers stands at 105 billion yuan [2].

The PBOC announces a new round of swap operations for these players. The CSRC asks major index constituents and tech champions to "actively buy back shares", and regulators are considering easing margin requirements [3].

The CSI 300 lost 8.5% in October, its worst month in more than ten years; it is down 13% since the start of the year. The STAR 50 index, which groups tech stocks, has dropped about 40% from its late-June peak [1][3].

The Shanghai Composite gained 1.1% on Monday, its biggest one-day rise since 27 August. But on Tuesday morning the CSI 300 and the Shanghai Composite were each down about 1%; one fund manager called the measures "below expectations" [3].

Key point: Beijing is turning an emergency measure into a permanent tool, which shows the state is counting on the stock market to support household and business confidence. When a company buys back its shares with money borrowed at 1%, it reduces the number of shares in circulation, which supports the price [2][1].

The mechanism is not new. On 24 September 2024, the PBOC launched a 300 billion yuan programme for share buybacks and another of at least 500 billion for purchases by non-bank institutions; the CSI 300 then had its biggest one-day rise since 2008 [4].
The problem, according to Breakingviews (Reuters), is that the support does not address the cause: company earnings must improve for the recovery to last [1].

If you hold a fund or ETF containing Chinese stocks, or buy products made in China, the health of China's stock market matters: it reflects confidence in the world's second-largest economy. To understand, not advice to buy or sell.

news.2026-11-03-algerie-locales-candidat: Algeria: three weeks before local elections, the opposition denounces the mass removal of its candidates

The municipal and wilaya (province) elections of 28 November 2026 will renew local assemblies for five years. The RCD, FFS, PT and Jil El Jadid denounce an administrative screening of their candidacies [1][2].
The 28 November vote is to renew municipal and wilaya assemblies for five years. Replacing rejected candidacies was possible until 28 October; appeals go through the administrative courts [1][3].
The FFS and the RCD point to Article 184 of the electoral law and speak of a targeted purge that would mainly hit list leaders and influential figures [2][4].
The electoral authority ANIE counts 162,864 candidates, against 134,140 in 2021, a rise of 21.4%. It has not published the number of candidates removed, and sitting mayors are among them [4].
Boycotting is risky: the 2026 law on parties exposes to judicial dissolution parties that field no candidates in two successive elections, which complicates building a united front [1][3].
Key point: can the opposition still weigh on the local vote if its candidates are removed before the election? The matter bears watching, as the figures on exclusions have not been published [4].
The choice is narrow for the parties: take part with depleted lists, or boycott at the risk of being dissolved, under the 2026 texts [1][3].
The Maghreb is a direct neighbour of Europe and a gas supplier: Algeria's political stability matters for European supplies and for relations with France.

news.2026-11-03-chili-activite-septembre: Chile: the economy grows 0.2% in September, held back by a 12.1% fall in mining output
Chile's central bank published its September activity indicator (Imacec) on Monday 2 November: +0.2% year on year, better than the flat reading expected, but copper mining fell 12.1% [1][2][3].
The Imacec, the monthly activity indicator of Chile's central bank, rose 0.2% in September 2026 compared with September 2025. The month had one more working day than last year [1][2].
Goods-producing sectors fell 2.0%, pulled down by a 12.1% drop in mining. The central bank attributes it to copper extraction, hit by lower ore grades and temporary operational shutdowns [2].
Non-mining activities rose 2.0%, driven by trade, services and industry; trade gained 4.5% [2][3].

The result beats the forecast of flat activity, after two consecutive monthly declines [3]. Chile's statistics institute INE puts fine copper output at 387,870 tonnes in September, 15.1% less than a year earlier [3].
Key point: Chile remains heavily dependent on copper. When mines produce less, the country's growth feels it at once, even if trade and services hold up [2][3].
Copper is used in cables, electric motors and batteries: Chilean output down 15.1% year on year in September feeds concerns about the metal's supply [3].
Copper goes into electric cars, wind turbines and power grids. If Chile's mines produce less, the metal's supply shrinks, which can weigh on the price of equipment that contains it.
